parole.testo: From Old Swedish -ilse, compared to Old West Norse -elsi; analog to -sla (verb suffix), agent suffix. Probably derived from Old Saxon -isli, -islo, from Proto-West Germanic *-islī. Also used to represent the Middle Low German suffix -nisse.
From Old Saxon alomahtig, from Proto-Germanic *alamahtīgaz (“almighty”).

parole.significato: a graven image (often a primitive or clumsy one)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bilæte, from Old Saxon biliði (“image”). Doublet of bild.
From Old Swedish frugha, from Old Saxon frūa. Doublet of fruga, Freja.
From Old Swedish frugha, from Old Saxon frūa. Doublet of fru, Fröja, Freja.

parole.significato: saint (a dead person recognised as holy)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hælghon, from Old Saxon hēlagon (“saints”), definite plural of the adjective hēlag (“holy”), from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz, cognate of German heilig, English holy. Compare Danish helgen.
From Old Swedish himil, from Old Saxon himil, from Proto-West Germanic *himil. Replaced Old Swedish himin, Old Norse himinn.

parole.significato: lovely, delightful, wonderful (very pleasant), (sometimes a better match for tone, as it can also sound casual) great
parole.testo: From Old Saxon hêrlik. Cf. German herrlich, Dutch heerlijk.
From Old Swedish krævet, from Old Saxon krevit, from Proto-West Germanic *krabit.
Unclear when the noun entered the language, from Old Saxon lēra or Middle Low German lēre. Compare Old Norse læra (verb).

From Old Swedish mænniskia, from Old Saxon mennisko, from the weak inflection of Proto-Germanic *manniskaz. Compare the synonym mänska (less common, informal), which is also from the weak inflection of *manniskaz, but via Old Norse menska and not via Old Saxon.
From Middle Low German plūme + -on (suffix appearing in the names of many berries and some fruits), from Old Saxon *plūma, from Proto-West Germanic *plūmā.

From Old Swedish thienst, þiǣnist, þiānist (“service, decoration of honor”), possibly from Old Saxon thionust or Old Frisian thianost, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz. Akin to German Dienst, Dutch dienst.

parole.significato: Inseparable verbal prefix that indicates an emphasizing meaning
parole.testo: From German er-, from Old High German ir-, and/or from Middle Low German er-, from Old Saxon ā-, both from Proto-Germanic *uz-.

parole.significato: a manger, a crib, a feeding trough for animals
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krubba, from Old Norse krubba, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ. Cognate with German Krippe, English crib. Alternatively, perhaps borrowed from Middle Low German krübbe, kribbe, from Old Saxon kribbia, from Proto-West Germanic *kribbjā, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ.

From Old Swedish krønika, krønik, from Middle Low German kröneke ~ kroneke, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “relating to time”), derived from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). Compare Danish and Norwegian krønike. It is not ruled out that the word was borrowed into Old Saxon ear

Borrowed from Low German rēling, regeling or from Dutch reeling, regeling, from Middle Low German regel, from Old Saxon *rigil, probably borrowed from Latin regula (“bar, rule”). Cognate of German Reling, English railing, Danish ræling.

parole.significato: to flush (let water (or another liquid) flow over, usually in order clean, and usually at pressure), (when cleaning) to…
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German spölen, from Old Saxon spōlian, from Proto-West Germanic *spōlijan. Compare the older byform spöla. The back vowel could stem from Low German past forms with Rückumlaut. Alternatively it could be from Middle Dutch influence. Cognate with Danish spule, Norwegian Bokmål

parole.significato: to think (think to oneself, have a thought (process) in one's head)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þænkia, from Middle Low German denken (“to perceive, think”), from Old Saxon thenkian. Possibly of Middle Low German origin (cf. Middle Low German adel), from Old Saxon ethiling, from Proto-West Germanic *aþuling, from Proto-Germanic *aþulingaz; alternatively from Old Norse ǫðlingr, ultimately from the same Proto-Germanic root.
